title: Search Closed Sources
summary: Closed sources are information collections that are not freely available: commercial threat intelligence subscriptions, paid data aggregation services, and criminal marketplaces. An adversary uses them because the same facts that help a defender also help an attacker, and because the material is often more current or more specific than anything published openly. Purchases of leaked credential sets, employee contact lists, and infrastructure detail are the typical goods. The activity happens off the victim estate entirely, so there is no victim-side telemetry at all. The only artefacts are financial and account trails held by the vendor or the marketplace, neither of which the defender can see. Defenders rarely observe the purchase itself. They observe the consequence, such as a credential stuffing wave that matches a third-party breach, and they infer the source from the tradecraft that follows.

beginner.definition: Closed sources are places that hold information you must pay for or that are not open to the public. They include paid threat report services and criminal marketplaces. This technique means an attacker buys or reads data from these places. The goal is to learn about you before attacking.
beginner.whyItMatters: Much of the useful information about your company is already for sale somewhere. Old passwords from other breaches, staff lists, and details about your systems all appear in such places. An attacker who buys them starts with a large advantage. You cannot see this in your logs because it happens somewhere else. Knowing this changes how you plan your defences.
howItWorks: The attacker identifies which paid or private sources hold data about your industry.
They buy a subscription, or they buy a single dataset from a criminal seller.
They search the material for your company name, your domains, and staff accounts.
They combine what they bought with free public information to fill the gaps.
They test any credentials they obtained, often by trying them on remote login services.
They use the results to choose a target and a method of entry.
beginner.example: Think of a market where traders sell old office keys collected over many years. Some keys are sold openly, and others only to members who pay a fee. A thief buys a box of keys and tries them on doors around the city. The building owner never learns that a key was sold. Closed source research works in that quiet way.
takeaways: Assume that information about your company is already for sale somewhere.
You will not see the purchase in your own logs, only its results.
React quickly to third-party breach notices that mention your accounts.

objectives: Define closed sources and distinguish them from openly available sources.
Explain why closed source data is valuable to an adversary.
Describe why closed source research produces no victim-side telemetry.
Explain how purchased credentials turn into attempted logins.
Outline a process for responding to third-party breach notifications.
